en: *Treatise on the Three Non-natures*, Fascicle One, excerpted from the *Treatise on Signlessness*.
Translated by Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha at Zhizhi Temple in Guangzhou.

The treatise states: In the "Chapter Establishing Emptiness," the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) has already been established; the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) has not yet been established. This is for the purpose of revealing the nature of phenomena.
"Because of emptiness, the chapter on the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena is taught.
The commentary asks:
Having previously taught the chapter on emptiness and subsequently teaching the chapter on the lack of intrinsic nature, what is intended to be accomplished?

Answer: It was stated previously that the Chapter on Emptiness (*śūnyatā-parivarta*) reveals the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), as it constitutes a distinct path that removes only the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

It was stated later that the Chapter on the Absence of Nature (*niḥsvabhāva-parivarta*) reveals the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), as it constitutes the universal path that removes both the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the afflictive obscurations.
Furthermore, there is another purpose: to eliminate the three false doctrines prevalent in the world:
first, the doctrine that victory in debate is supreme, such as the Lokāyatika and Sāṃkhya treatises;
second, the doctrine that extensive learning is supreme, such as the four Vedas and the Itihāsa and Purāṇa treatises.
The three [types of] correct practice are considered superior theories, such as those taught in the vehicles of the two [vehicles] and so forth.

Now, by expounding the two kinds of emptiness, these three theories are eliminated. First, the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is taught to eliminate the two former theories of the non-Buddhists;

next, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is taught to eliminate the latter two—the biased attachments of the two vehicles and even the erroneous attachments of the non-Buddhists—thereby revealing true correct practice. It is because one relies on this practice that the ultimate, peerless state is attained.
Furthermore, the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is taught to refute false doctrines, while the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is taught to establish the true Dharma.
To extensively clarify the function of this treatise—such as its application regarding the eighteen schools—it was composed in order to manifest this utility.
This is the first section, "Clarifying the Function.
The treatise says:
An external questioner asks: In what phenomena is this lack of intrinsic nature established?
One should first establish this doctrine.
If it is explained in this way, then the principle of signlessness (animitta) will correspond to its object, and both real and unreal objects will then be visible.
He replied:
All phenomena do not transcend the three natures: first, the imagined nature; second, the dependent nature; and third, the perfected nature.
The imagined nature refers to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as manifested by names and conventions; it is the aspect of consciousness that resembles objects.

The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) refers to the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of phenomena based upon causes and conditions; that is, because it arises from internal faculties as its causal basis and internal objects as its conditions within the realm of deluded consciousness.
Reality (*tattva*) refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) of phenomena.
"Phenomena" here refers to the two natures: the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*).

"Suchness" refers to the non-existence of these two natures. Because the imagined nature lacks any essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it is non-existent; because the dependent nature lacks arising (*utpāda*), it is non-existent. Since both of these non-existences are devoid of change, they are called "suchness. Therefore, this suchness is termed reality.
This is the second section on "Correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*), which establishes the names.

Next, based on these three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*) are explained; through these three absences of nature, one should understand the principle of the single absence of nature.
Regarding the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it is said to be "without nature" by virtue of the non-existence of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*). Why is this?
Because that which appears as a characteristic does not exist in reality; therefore, the imputed nature has the absence of characteristics as its very nature.
Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is called "natureless" by virtue of its lack of nature in terms of arising. Why is this?
This arising is established through the power of conditions and does not arise of itself; that power of conditions is precisely the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Since the essence of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) does not exist, its arising cannot be established because it lacks the power of conditions; therefore, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) has non-arising as its essence.
With respect to the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), it is said to be without essence because the perfected nature itself is without essence.
Why is this? Because this principle is the ultimate reality.
Since all phenomena are, by virtue of this principle, of one and the same natureless character (*niḥsvabhāva*), true reality has non-nature as its very nature.
The commentary states:

Regarding the nature of reality (*tathatā*), it is said to be "without intrinsic nature" because reality is devoid of intrinsic nature. This nature of reality is not some separate phenomenon; rather, the very absence of the two previous natures is itself the nature of reality, for reality is characterized by being signless and unarisen.

All conditioned phenomena do not transcend these two natures: the imagined and the dependent. Since these two natures are ultimately without characteristics and without arising, by this principle all dharmas are of one and the same absence of nature.
This single absence of nature is truly non-existent and truly existent.
It is truly non-existent because these two—the imagined and the dependent—are absent;
it is truly existent because these two—the imagined and the dependent—are non-existent. Therefore, it cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist.

It cannot be said that it exists like the five sensory objects, nor can it be said that it does not exist like the horns of a rabbit; thus, it is neither of the nature of existence nor of the nature of non-existence, and is therefore called "the nature of the absence of nature" (*abhāva-svabhāvatā*).
Furthermore, taking non-existence as its nature is called the "nature of non-existence," which is precisely the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
If these three natures were all established truths, then the first two natures would be established conventional truths, because their essence is actually non-established yet is posited as existent;

and the true nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) would be the established ultimate truth, for it is named the ultimate truth by means of negating the two existences and establishing the two non-existences.
Returning to investigate this nature, one finds it free from both existence and non-existence; therefore, it is not established.
The three natures of non-being are all non-established.
This constitutes the third aspect, clarifying the essential characteristics of the three types of natures.
The Treatise says:
Having thus explained the characteristics of these three natures as being without intrinsic nature, it is now necessary to explain the principles by which they are established.
As for the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it has no substantial essence or characteristic.
Why is this? Because this nature is not subsumed within the five aggregates (*skandha*).
If a phenomenon were existent, it would not fail to be included among the five aggregates.

The five repositories (pañca-kośa) are: first, the characteristic (lakṣaṇa); second, the name (nāman); third, discrimination (vikalpa); fourth, suchness (tathatā); and fifth, non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna).
Regarding the "characteristic": it refers to the categories of all phenomena (dharma) as that upon which names, phrases, and syllables depend.
"Name" refers to the words, phrases, and phonemes within the categories of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
"Discrimination" refers to the mind and mental factors of the three realms.
"Suchness" refers to the sphere of noble wisdom manifested by the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Regarding non-conceptual wisdom: by means of this wisdom, all noble ones (ārya) are able to penetrate suchness (tathatā).
Among these five dharmas, the first three belong to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), while the latter two are suchness.
All phenomena do not transcend these five.

If the nature of the imagined character (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) were an existent entity, it would necessarily be subsumed within these five; since it is not so subsumed, we know that its nature is non-existent.
The opponent says:
"If this dharma has no essential nature or characteristics, how can it be differentiated?
The respondent replies:
There are merely names without corresponding meanings. Why is this?
Just as the world establishes names based on meanings, ordinary beings cling to these names and differentiate the nature of meanings, asserting that the name is itself the nature of the meaning.
This is a perversion; therefore, there is only conceptual construction and no substantial reality.
The opponent asks:
How is it known that this conceptual construction is a false attachment?
Answer: Because both these names and their meanings are adventitious. Why is this so?
A name is adventitious within its meaning because it does not belong to the category of that meaning.
Meaning is also adventitious within a name,
because it does not belong to the same category as the name.
The opponent says:
How is it known that these two are mutually adventitious?
The answer is:
this principle can be understood through three points.
First, knowledge does not arise prior to the name.

For example, regarding names established by worldly convention: if this name were identical to the essential nature of the object, then the object should not be apprehended before one has heard the name.
Since one has already apprehended the meaning prior to seeing the name and before it has been assigned,
and furthermore, if the name were identical to the meaning, one should have already acquired the name at the very moment the meaning was apprehended;
because this is not the case, we know that the name is adventitious.
Second, because a single meaning has many names.
If the name were identical to the nature of the meaning, then since a single entity may have various names, it would follow that there must be as many entities as there are names.
If there were multiple entities corresponding to multiple names, then contradictory phenomena would be established in a single location.
This principle is contradicted by direct perception (*pramāṇa*), as such a state of affairs does not exist; therefore, it is known that [the name] is adventitious (*āgantuka*).
Third, because names are not fixed.
If a name were identical to the nature of its referent, then since names are not fixed, the substance of the referent would likewise have to be not fixed. Why is this so?
Alternatively, because the name of this object is applied to that object, it is known that the name is not fixed to the object.
Since this is not the case, we know that [the name] is merely adventitious (*āgantuka*).
Furthermore, you say:
This name exists within the meaning.
As for its existence within the meaning:
does it exist in that which has meaning, or in that which lacks meaning?
If it exists in the object, the previous three difficulties are established once again.
If it does not exist in the object, then both name and object are adventitious; this is definitively established.
The opponent says:
Meanings and names are not produced by conceptual construction. Why is this?
Because a real name can manifest a real meaning, just as a lamp that actually exists illuminates a jar that actually exists; therefore, both name and meaning are not conceptual constructions.
Answer: This interpretation is not correct. Why is this so?
Because it illuminates that which is not equal. If, as you say,
the referent (artha) actually exists and the name is used to manifest that referent— just as a lamp illuminates a form— then...
This argument is not established.
Why? Because one must first apprehend the meaning before establishing a name; as long as the meaning has not been apprehended, a name cannot be established.
Since a name is established only after an object has first been apprehended, if even the apprehension itself cannot fully comprehend the object, how much less can its name do so?
This is not the case with a lamp illuminating an object.

It is because of the lamp that one can perceive objects; it is not the case that one first perceives the object and only then requires the lamp. Therefore, the principle of illumination is not symmetrical.
The commentary states:

"To say that even grasping cannot yet perceive the meaning" means that consciousness first apprehends the meaning, and subsequently grasps whether it is blue or yellow, or whether it is correct or incorrect; it is only after this grasping that a name is established.

If one were to apprehend an object through the act of grasping, then it would follow that consciousness has already apprehended the object even before the grasping occurs; therefore, it cannot be the case that the object is apprehended by depending on grasping. Since the name exists only after grasping, how could it possibly apprehend [the object]?
Furthermore, if a name were capable of manifesting its meaning, then when others do not yet recognize that name, they should not hear the name and fail to grasp its meaning.

It would be like the case where, by means of a lamp illuminating forms, this person is able to clearly perceive those forms because of the lamp, while other people cannot see those forms because of it.
This principle does not apply here, because a definitive cause can manifest color through illumination.
Manifesting meaning by means of names is not like this; therefore, the sense of "illumination" is not equivalent in the two cases.
The Commentary states:
The opponent says:

If you claim that one distinguishes an object by means of a name, yet in reality there is no object to be distinguished, and therefore there is no object within the name and no name within the object, such that both are adventitious; [then we respond as follows].
This interpretation is not correct. Why?

If a person holds that the name is distinct from the meaning and the meaning is distinct from the name, then since this person would have no cognitive inversion, they should have no biased attachment regarding the meaning; nor should they experience feelings of sorrow or joy upon hearing descriptions of the good or the bad, because the name and the meaning would be unrelated.
Because one gives rise to thoughts of sorrow or joy upon hearing names of good or evil, one knows that the meaning of "name" is consistent [with its object] and cannot be a guest.
You should know that the notion of a "guest" is your own perversion.
Answer: This interpretation is not correct. Why is this so?
This perverse attachment arises from long-standing habituation to inversions; it has no bearing on the correspondence between names and their referents.
Even if a person maintains that names and referents are distinct, they still cannot avoid this perverse attachment regarding the relationship between names and their referents.
Why is this? It is because of the long-term habituation to the熏習 (vāsanā) of names and conventions.

Necessarily, through this gateway of phenomena, a discriminating mind arises that gives rise to false and perverse attachments. Just as ordinary people—even those with right view—know that this body is merely an aggregate of formations such as form and so forth, yet because their habituation to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is firm, they cannot avoid the perverse attachment to a personal self within their own and others' continuums.

Thus, the conceptual differentiation of names and meanings is a biased attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which is precisely a perversion (*viparyāsa*), because it superimposes [existence] upon that which is non-existent.
Just as there is a biased attachment to a personal self (*pudgalagrāha*), one should know that the biased attachment to names and meanings is a perversion regarding phenomena.
Since these are indeed inversions, how could such inversions arise without being fetters?

Therefore, through the perfuming of perverse attachments, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) becomes a seed, which is capable of producing the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) as a future fruit.
This perverse attachment is precisely the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which serves as the cause for the future dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, based on this future fruit of the dependent nature, there further arises the inversion of dharma-attachment in the future; that is, with the dependent nature acting as the cause, it is able to produce the future conceptual construction as the fruit.
Thus, because they act as mutual causes for one another, birth and death constantly arise in an uninterrupted succession.
This concludes the fourth section, the establishment of the three natures.
The explanation of the meaning of the establishment of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is now complete.
There are another six kinds of distinctions; next, the categories and sub-classifications of this nature will be explained.
Now, there are six types of distinctions within this *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature):

first, the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), which refers to the discrimination of the essential characteristics of the aggregates (*skandhas*) such as form (*rūpa*), and which is apprehended solely through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The five consciousnesses can only directly apprehend the five sense objects, and even the mental consciousness can only directly apprehend mental phenomena (*dharma*) without performing various conceptual discriminations regarding them; therefore, they are called "intrinsic discrimination" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), because they directly apprehend their essential natures.
Second is the discrimination of distinctions, which refers to such categories as "matter that is visible" and "matter that is invisible.
Matter is visible, whereas the five sense objects—odor, flavor, and so forth—are not seen by the eye.
Thus, because various differentiations arise within a single intrinsic nature, it is called "differentiation of distinctions.
Third is "differentiation of cognitive awareness," which refers to seeing a phenomenon before one and immediately recognizing its name and being able to explain it to others.
Because one has already recognized the name for oneself and is further able to cause others to recognize it as well, it is called "discrimination through conscious awareness.

Fourth is "latent discrimination" (*anuśaya-vikalpa*): this refers to seeing an object before one and not recognizing its name, nor being able to describe it; therefore, it is called "latent discrimination."
Fifth is the discrimination of application (*prayoga-vikalpa*), which further comprises five types:

first, discrimination following attachment; second, discrimination of aversion and recollection; third, discrimination of conjunction; fourth, discrimination of separation; and fifth, discrimination following equanimity.
Because these five types of discrimination give rise to the afflictions of the three poisons, they are termed "preparatory application" (*prayoga*).
Combining these five with the preceding four, all are distinguished according to their specific meanings.
The sixth is conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), which is further divided into two types:
first, that with names; second, that without names.

"With names" refers to the grasping at things as being truly thus—whether as form up to consciousness, or as conditioned or unconditioned, permanent or impermanent, wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—and all such attachments constitute conceptual differentiation with names.
That which is without name refers to: "What is this thing? "How is it?
and "For what reason?"
Why is this so? This fourfold analysis consists of: first, seeking the essential nature;
second, seeking the cause—that is, by what causes and conditions such a thing exists.
Third, the differentiation of the essence through seeking;
fourth, the differentiation of the cause through investigation.
These four are all conceptualizations devoid of names.

These are the five kinds of conceptualizing the intrinsic nature of objects based on names. Furthermore, there are five kinds of conceptualized intrinsic natures: first, the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of objects based on names;

second, the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of names based on objects; third, the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of names based on names; fourth, the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of objects based on objects; and fifth, the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of both names and objects based on both names and objects.

First, regarding the differentiation of the intrinsic nature of objects based on names: this refers to the determination that "this category is form," which is established by the essential nature of form; and so on, up to "this category is feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness," which is established by the essential nature of consciousness.
The commentary states:

This means that this person, having previously not yet realized the meaning but having first acquired the name "form" (*rūpa*), hears it said that the characteristic of form is such as having physical resistance, being graspable, and possessing such qualities as decay and destruction; thus, it is designated as "form."

Later, when this person sees the substance, categories, and characteristics of form, they recognize it as form just as they previously heard described; thus, it is precisely by means of names that one is able to differentiate the essential nature of form.

This applies even to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*): first one obtains its name but has not yet seen its substance; later, when one encounters its substance, one recognizes it as feeling (*vedanā*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), just as was previously heard.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the statement that "the distinction of names based on meaning constitutes their intrinsic nature," this means that one determines whether a given category may be designated as "form" (*rūpa*) or not, and so on up to whether it may be designated as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) or not; it is by first apprehending the meaning that one subsequently distinguishes and establishes its name.

Regarding the third [type of discrimination], discrimination of the intrinsic nature based on names (*nāman*): this refers to when one has acquired the name "form" (*rūpa*), yet does not yet recognize the category to which that name belongs; one further reflects upon and studies its etymological interpretation. This is called discrimination of the name based on the name. The same applies even to the case where, having recognized the name, one seeks out its specific etymological category.

Regarding the fourth [type], the discrimination of the intrinsic nature of meaning based on meaning: this refers to the case where, before the name for a form has been acquired, one discriminates the category of form due to an indeterminate name.

It is like a person who does not yet know the name of an object but, upon seeing its physical substance, discriminates that this substance is distinct from other objects, yet does not know for certain what specific thing it is.
Because their definitive names cannot be established, they are merely designated by relying on their meanings to differentiate those meanings.

This is also like what is seen by infants who do not yet recognize names, or the objects obtained in the stage of non-conceptual consciousness, such as the five sensory consciousnesses; in all these cases, one perceives the meaning without perceiving the name.
Fifth, the differentiation of names and meanings based on names and meanings refers to this category [of phenomena] having form (*rūpa*) as its substance; this form is itself the name.

Just as a person who has already recognized a name and its meaning subsequently differentiates again those previously recognized names and meanings, saying, "This is the substance of form" and "This is the name for form," and so on, up to this category having consciousness (*vijñāna*) as its substance; this consciousness is itself the name.
All such cases as these are termed "discriminating name and meaning based on name and meaning.

These five types of discrimination are an expansion of the first of the six [types of discrimination], namely, "discrimination of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*). Because it was explained briefly previously, it was simply called "discrimination of intrinsic nature"; because it is now explained extensively, the five kinds of intrinsic nature are distinguished.
Thus, the preceding six and the subsequent five are all termed the categories of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
Having completed the explanation of the categories of the imagined nature, next the function of the imagined nature will be explained.

This nature of discrimination can differentiate the former six and the latter five; now, in order to manifest the specific functions of these six and five types of discrimination, there are eight kinds of discrimination that can perform three types of activities.
The three categories of phenomena are:
first, the category of conceptual proliferation; second, the category of the view of self and the conceit of "I am"; and third, the category of afflictions such as desire.
The eight kinds of discrimination are:

First is the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*). This refers to categories such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; "form" is the intrinsic nature of form itself, while the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are the intrinsic natures of the other four aggregates.

That is to say, it includes the first of the five types of discrimination previously mentioned—discrimination of meaning based on names—and the first of the six types of discrimination, namely the discrimination of intrinsic nature. All such instances are termed the discrimination of intrinsic nature.

Second is the discrimination of distinctions (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*), which refers to the immeasurable varieties of discrimination regarding categories such as form—such as being visible or invisible, obstructive or non-obstructive—and so forth; all these depend upon the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), and are thus called the discrimination of distinctions.

Among the three categories, there is the discrimination that clings to a portion; this refers to clinging to the aggregates such as form, and to names such as "self," "sentient being," "life-span," "nourisher," and "experiencer"—conventions established by common consensus—and clinging to these while giving rise to discrimination.
Furthermore, within a collection of many dharmas, one grasps the collection itself as the cause—such as a house, an army, a chariot, food, clothing, drink, and so forth.

Names such as these are all established through conventional agreement; to grasp them and thereby give rise to conceptual discrimination is called "the discrimination that grasps a part within a collection."
These two are precisely the internal and external conceptualizations; the former is the attachment to a person (*pudgala*), and the latter is the attachment to phenomena (*dharma*).
The commentary states:
"Common convention" refers to names established through worldly usage, all of which are produced by mutual agreement and intended to bring about a uniform understanding.
The Treatise says:

The four types of self-discrimination refer to this category which is with outflows and with grasping; it is a long-standing attachment to a self that has been repeatedly cultivated through habituation. From this perverse attachment and habituation, and taking the basis of the view of a self as its object, one gives rise to false discrimination; this is called self-discrimination.
The commentary states:
This "category" refers to that which possesses outflows (*sāsrava*) and grasping (*sopādāna*). This "category" is precisely the *ālayavijñāna*, which serves as the root of all afflictions.
"Possessing outflows" is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*).
That which possesses grasping is precisely craving.

Since the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) of past afflictions have been extinguished, they cannot be distinguished by the names of various delusions; they are collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*), because it is capable of obstructing the clarity of wisdom.
This ignorance can act as the cause for all afflictions and can cause one to transmigrate through birth and death; therefore, it is called an "outflow" (*āsrava*).

As the Sāṃkhyas say, it is called an outflow because it flows into birth and death, because the mental outflows (*citta-āsrava*) flow forth in continuous succession, and because it is not held by any person; thus, it is termed an outflow.

"Grasping" (upādāna) refers to the fruit of the category of existence-tendencies (bhava-āsrava). Because the cause has passed away into the past, it is called an "existence-tendency"; because the fruit has arisen and exists within the present continuum, it is called "grasping."
This refers precisely to the seeds of latent desire (*anuśaya-rāga*) within the present continuum.

If all afflictions (*kleśa*) are said to be "outflows" (*āsrava*) and "grasping" (*upādāna*) while residing in the present continuum, then "outflows" are the four outflows, and "grasping" is the four graspings.

Thus, these distinct explanations regarding the outflows (*āsrava*), grasping (*upādāna*), and so forth, do not depart from the fundamental consciousness; therefore, it is said that this category consists of the outflows and grasping.

Regarding the phrase "long-term self-clinging repeatedly based on habitual practice," this is a general statement that such afflictions as the outflows and grasping have existed since beginningless time; hence, it is called "long-term."
There are three types of self-grasping:
first, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); second, active states of mind (*paryavasthāna*); and third, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Regarding the term "repeatedly," this clarifies that the latent tendency of self-grasping repeatedly clings to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its basis.
"Latent tendency" (*vāsanā*) refers to the habitual arising of the ego-clinging of the manifest mind;
"habituation" (*abhyāsa*) refers to the frequent arising of the ego-clinging of the manifest impregnations.
Latent tendencies and manifest states are internal afflictions; upon attaining the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), these delusions are extinguished.

Vāsanās are formed through long-term habituation and are not primary afflictions; therefore, they have not yet been extinguished at the time one attains arhatship, but can only be gradually dispelled upon realizing the suchness of dharmas.

These three forms of self-grasping all rely upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). Regarding the statement that they "arise from false discrimination by taking as their object the category upon which the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) relies," this clarifies that the fundamental consciousness possesses two meanings by which it serves as the basis for these three types of view of a self-body:
first, it acts as the seed that produces the view of a self-body; second, it functions as the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of the view of a self-body, causing false self-grasping to arise.
To speak correctly, because this fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) arises by taking [the self] as its object, it is called "discrimination of self.
The treatise says:

"The fivefold discrimination of 'mine' refers to this category being with outflows (*sāsrava*) and grasping (*upādāna*). Due to long-term habitual attachment to the notion of 'mine,' from this perverse habituation, one takes as an object the category that serves as the basis for the view of 'mine' and gives rise to false discrimination; this is called the discrimination of 'mine.'"

The nature of the apprehended object does not differ from that of the fourth [type of discrimination]; the only difference is that it can further discriminate between the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-grāha*).
The sixth is the discrimination of craving (*tṛṣṇā-vikalpa*), which refers to false discrimination based on agreeable and pure categories; this is called the discrimination of craving.

Seventh is the discrimination of aversion and recollection (*pratighānusmaraṇa-vikalpa*); this refers to false discrimination that takes as its object unclean things that are loathsome, and is thus called the discrimination of aversion and recollection.

Eighth is the discrimination of neither-love-nor-aversion (*anunaya-pratighābhāva-vikalpa*); this refers to taking as its object things that are neither lovely nor loathsome, and is called the discrimination of neither-love-nor-aversion by way of being the opposite of the preceding two discriminations.
Briefly stated, there are only two kinds of conceptualization:
first, the basis of conceptualization; second, the object of conceptualization.

Among the eight types of conceptualization, three—namely, the conceptualization of intrinsic nature, the conceptualization of specific difference, and the conceptualization of grasping at a collection—are able to serve as the basis for the conceptualization of proliferation and as the objects of the conceptualization of proliferation.

Why is this? Because the discrimination that arises based on these categories of names, concepts, and expressions, as well as the discrimination that is perfumed by names, concepts, and expressions, is called "discrimination of conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca-vikalpa*).
Within these three categories, because they are conditioned by the three names, various characteristics repeatedly arise and function.
Such conceptualization is called *prapañca* (proliferation); it takes the three categories as its basis, the three names as its object, and conceptualization itself as its essence.

The objective basis (*ālambana*) is the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), while discursive conceptualization (*prapañca-vikalpa*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The commentary states:
among the eight types of conceptualization, the first three are termed "discursive proliferation" (*prapañca*).
Each of these three types of discrimination is itself the basis, the object, and the essence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Why is this? Because within each of the three types of discrimination, there exists both the subject and the object.
The capacity [of conceptualization] is the very essence of proliferation (*prapañca*); that which is grasped therein is twofold, namely:
categories (*jāti*) and names (*nāman*). Categories refer to the three types of objective categories; names refer to the various designations for those three categories.
Therefore, one relies upon meaning as the support and takes names as the objective sphere; by taking these names as the gateway to the Dharma, one grasps the categories of meaning.

Precisely because that which is grasped serves as the support and that which is objectified serves as the objective sphere, it is said that one relies on these categories and conditions the conceptual discrimination arising from names, perceptions, and speech.
"Conceptualizing through speech" means that the mind conceives of this name and speaks this name; hence it is called "conceptualizing through speech.
This refers to discrimination as the basis upon which conceptualization and speech rely.

The inclusion of the terms "perception" (*saṃjñā*) and "speech" (*abhilāpa*) here is for the purpose of indicating that names (*nāman*) possess degrees of coarseness and subtlety: the name is subtle, perception is slightly coarse, and speech is the coarsest of all. Therefore, these three terms are employed to designate and differentiate the three levels [of expression].
First, the discrimination of intrinsic nature directly clarifies the essential substance of phenomena such as form; because this meaning is subtle, it is designated by the name "name" (*nāman*).
Next, the discrimination of differentiation clarifies the distinctions within that substance; because these are relatively coarse, they are designated by the name "perception" (*saṃjñā*).

Within that collection, there is one type of conceptualization called "clinging to distinctions," such as [the notions of] a jar or a house; this is the most coarse, and therefore it is designated by its verbal expression.

Regarding the statement that "conceptualization perfumed by names, perceptions, and speech is called 'conceptualization of proliferation'": because one gives rise to conceptualization by taking those three as objects, the conceptualized object possesses the sense of being perfumed by the conceptualizing subject; thus, the conceptualizing subject is itself the conceptualization of proliferation.

Regarding the phrase "within the three categories, taking the three names as objects, repeatedly giving rise to various modes of appearance," this clarifies that by relying upon the three categories and taking the three names as the gateway of the Dharma (*dharmamukha*), one repeatedly gives rise to various modes of appearance.
The conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) based on the support of objective spheres (*viṣaya*) is in essence one, yet possesses three functional aspects.
The treatise says:
Next, [regarding] "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*):
These two types of discrimination can act as the basis for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and all other views;
they can act as the basis for the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) and all other forms of pride (*māna*).
The commentary states:

These two types of discrimination should also be clarified by analogy with what precedes; that is, they serve as the objective basis (*ālambana*) and the essential substance (*svabhāva*) of discrimination.

Since these have already been explained, they can be understood through analogy and need not be analyzed further; therefore, I shall simply clarify how they give rise to the subsequent view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and act as the root of all views.
Due to the grasping at a self, various views arise; the grasping at "mine" can act as the basis for the conceit "I am" and for the various types of pride.
The treatise states:
Subsequently, there are the two opposites of love and hatred; these three types of discrimination can give rise to desire, aversion, ignorance, and so forth.
The commentary states:
These three types of discrimination are themselves the three poisons; therefore, they are able to give rise to all three poisons.
The treatise says:
These eight kinds of discrimination can produce three categories of objects of enjoyment.

The first three constitute the category of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); the next two constitute the category of self-view and self-conceit (*asmimāna*); and the final three constitute the category of afflictions such as desire.
First, these six kinds of discrimination manifest and encompass the meaning of all phenomena; no discrimination exists outside of these six.
They generally comprise three categories of meaning:

self-nature and differentiation—these two are the basis of discrimination; awareness, latent tendencies, and application—these three are the essence of discrimination; and finally, names are the objects of discrimination.
Therefore, the six categories of encompassing factors are fully exhausted.
*Bodha* (awakening) and *anuśaya* (latent tendencies) pertain to all three natures (*tridhātu*), whereas *prayoga* (preparatory application) is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).
There are five types of separation from these manifest afflictions (*paryavasthāna*):
Following attachment gives rise to greed; following aversion gives rise to hatred; following equanimity gives rise to ignorance—these three constitute the essence of the afflictions.
Conjoining and distancing are the functions of the afflictions: through greed one conjoins, and through hatred one distances oneself.
Due to ignorance (*avidyā*), both of these functions are established collectively, rather than being assigned distinct capacities.

Greed (*rāga*) brings about conjunction because it draws in objects; hatred (*dveṣa*) brings about separation because it rejects objects. Since there is drawing in and rejection only because ignorance exists, ignorance thus establishes both functions collectively.

Next, based on the five kinds of discrimination—such as the discrimination of meaning according to names—and so forth, this is intended to reveal the basis and object of discrimination, as well as the distinctions between their respective bases and objects.

However, the nature of discrimination subsumes the latter eight types of discrimination; these are presented to reveal the three kinds of obstructive phenomena: namely, the grasping at intrinsic nature, the grasping at distinctions, and the grasping at the unity within a collection. These three types of discrimination can give rise to mental afflictions and constitute the obstruction to omniscience (*sarvajñāvaraṇa*).
The two conceptualizations of "I" and "mine" give rise to the afflictions of the flesh, acting as obstacles to liberation.
The three conceptualizations of the "lovely," the "hateful," and their opposites give rise to the afflictions of the skin, acting as obstacles to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

These three afflictions correspond to three categories of phenomena: mental affliction corresponds to the category of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); fleshly affliction corresponds to the category of self-conceit (*asmimāna*); and skin-like affliction corresponds to the category of defilements such as sensual desire (*kāma*).
These three categories of phenomena are of the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
To speak briefly of their conceptualization (*vikalpa*), they do not exceed three types:
first, the basis of conceptualization; second, the essence of conceptualization; and third, the object of conceptualization.
If one speaks of the substance of discrimination, it refers to the mind and mental factors of the three realms.

There is no separate substance for their support or their objects; rather, that which resembles the category of sense-objects serves as the support, and the name of that which resembles the category of sense-objects serves as the object.
Next, the delusions of characteristics (*nimitta-kleśa*) and the delusions of heavy entanglement (*dausthulya-kleśa*) are distinguished.

If the nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arises, it can bind sentient beings with two types of delusion: first, the delusion of characteristics; second, the delusion of heavy entanglement.

The delusion of characteristics (*nimitta*) is the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), while the delusion of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) is the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The reason these two types of delusion can be established is that they are established by grasping at the nature of dependence on others as being the nature of conceptual construction.
The commentary states:

To call the nature of discrimination "defilement of appearances" (nimitta-kleśa), "appearance" refers to a characteristic form; it is described as defilement because that characteristic form serves as the causal condition for defilement, and is thus termed defilement.

However, while it is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) that constitutes the actual affliction, when one speaks of its gravity, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is merely the object-condition for affliction; because it is described as the affliction [in this sense], it is said to be light.
The dependent nature is the very essence of the affliction itself; therefore, it is described as coarse and heavy (*dausthulya*).
Because the afflictions of conceptual signs obstruct non-conceptual wisdom by causing one to differentiate characteristics that do not accord with the object of non-conceptualization;
because the afflictions of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) directly induce future rebirth and the acquisition of various sufferings and so forth.
Since these two necessarily exist in mutual dependence, it is said that the two delusions bind sentient beings.
The Treatise says:
If a person does not fail to perceive these two natures, they will immediately attain liberation from these two delusions.
"Non-attainment" refers to the non-attainment of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Since this nature is eternally without substance, there is nothing to be attained.
"Non-perception" refers to the non-perception of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Although the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) possesses substantiality, because the mind does not take its characteristics as an object, this nature also does not exist [for that mind], and is thus said to be "not seen.
The reason why this nature must necessarily be not seen is due to two kinds of paths:
first, the path of vision (darśana-mārga); second, the path of abandonment (prahāṇa-mārga).
Because conceptualization ceases through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is said that "it is not attained.
Because the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*) is extinguished through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is said that "it is not seen.
The commentary states:
In the past, because one had not yet seen the truth, false discrimination arose; to claim that what does not exist exists is called "false view.
By means of this false view, one is able to obstruct the path of remedy.

Now that the principle has been seen, one realizes that what was previously perceived does not exist; thus it is said that the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is simply non-existent.
Because this correct path can eliminate former false views, it is said that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is extinguished.

In the past, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) were considered to have two distinct entities; now, seeing that the two paths are eliminated, they are likewise one and not two.
The Treatise says:
This concludes the four meanings establishing the function of the imagined nature.
This section establishes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The essential characteristics of this nature have already been explained as before; now, in order to establish this nature, the principles of its establishment are set forth.
This nature does not have verbal expression as its essence.
Why is this? Because verbal expression must necessarily have a basis upon which it relies.
If it were not established by relying on the designations for the categories of disordered consciousness, such a thing would be impossible.
Were it otherwise, since the categories upon which it depends do not exist, the designations spoken of could not be established.
If that were so, there would be no duality; because there is no duality, there would be no category of delusion; and because there is no category of delusion, two faults would follow:
first, liberation would occur spontaneously without effort; second, neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa could be manifested.
Because these two faults do not exist, one should know that the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) certainly exists.
The commentary states:

Here, it is said that names and conventions must have a basis; they take the dependent nature as their support. It is because the dependent nature exists that names and conventions can be established; if this nature did not exist, there would be nothing to establish them.

Therefore, it is clarified here that the categories of the basis (*āśraya*) differ from those previously mentioned; previously, the categories of the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) were taken as the basis for names and expressions.
The treatise asks:
What are the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of this nature?
Answer: It consists solely of the category of signs (*nimitta*) and the category of coarse heaviness and afflictions (*dauṣṭhulya-kleśa*). Question:
How is it that these types are said to depend on others?
The answer is:
because they mutually serve as causes and conditions for one another’s co-arising.

The reason for this is that the state of *dausthulya* (dysfunction) is established through the condition of characteristics (*nimitta*), and because the category of *dausthulya* is established through its own conditioning, these two categories are called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Why is this? Because they do not possess distinct natures, both are termed "dependent nature" (paratantra-svabhāva); yet, in terms of their specific meanings, they are ultimately not the same. Question:
If that is so, why is this nature called "unborn" (anutpāda) by virtue of being unborn?
The answer is:
it is called "unborn" because it arises through the power of others.
Since it has no essence, it cannot produce by itself.
Because it lacks both cause and essence, there is therefore no production. Question:
Why is this nature not known as either existent or non-existent?
The answer is:
because this nature does not exist in the manner it is conceptualized, it cannot be said to exist; yet, since it is not categorically non-existent, it cannot be said to be non-existent either.
Because it exists in this manner, it is not non-existent; because it is not unilaterally non-existent, it is not non-non-existent.

If one understands this meaning, then all types of designations may be applied: it may be said to exist, it may be said to be non-existent, it may be said to both exist and be non-existent, or it may be said to neither exist nor be non-existent; none of these are mutually contradictory.
Question: When it is said that "this exists," does this refer to the existence of a substantial entity or the existence of a conventional designation? Answer:
Because it possesses two meanings, it can be said to exist:
it does not exist in the manner [of ultimate reality], thus it is called "existence by designation" (prajñaptisat);
yet it is not entirely non-existent, thus it is called "existence as a thing" (vastusat), meaning that there is a thing.
Question: Since it has been stated that [things] exist, does this refer to conventional existence or to ultimate existence? Answer:
All of these exist conventionally.
Why? Because they are not objects of non-conceptual [wisdom].
Question: What are the characteristics of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)? Answer:
The conventional truth has three aspects, namely: discourse on the self, discourse on phenomena, and discourse on things.
Discourse on the self refers to [concepts such as] the self, sentient beings, life-span, persons, humans and devas, men and women, and so forth.
The teaching of phenomena refers to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The teaching of things refers to seeing, hearing, arising, and ceasing.
These are termed the conventional; it is through the conventional that this category of the dependent nature is established.
The previously mentioned nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) also has four aspects:
first, establishing existence; second, establishing essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); third, establishing functional efficacy (*kāritra*); and fourth, establishing distinctions.
The extensive clarification of its essence and characteristics has already been explained as previously stated; the detailed elucidation of its functional activity will be explained separately later.

Herein, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is first clarified because one wishes to demonstrate that this nature exists; therefore, the functional activities such as the category of afflictions are cited, which is why these activities are briefly mentioned prior to the essence and characteristics.
The Treatise says:
What is the essence of this nature?
Below, its essential characteristics will be briefly explained once more.
Question: What are the characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)?
The following clarifies the distinctions within this nature.

The sevenfold suchness (*tathatā*) possesses many meanings; within the suchness of arising, it clarifies the meaning of the distinction between the dependent and the imagined natures, and the absence of temporal sequence in the arising and ceasing of cause and effect.
Regarding ultimate truth, it refers to the sevenfold suchness:
first, arising; second, characteristics; third, consciousness; fourth, the basis; fifth, erroneous practice; sixth, purification; and seventh, correct practice.
That which is "suchness throughout one's life" refers to the fact that conditioned phenomena have neither beginning nor end.
Conditioned phenomena are subsumed under only two natures: namely, the imagined (parikalpita) and the dependent (paratantra).
This dharma has neither priority nor posteriority, and generally consists of three types.

First, regarding the two natures, one establishes their lack of priority and posteriority: if it is said that the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) comes first, there would be no *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), and thus the dependent nature would not be established;
if it is said that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* comes first, there would be no *paratantra-svabhāva*, and thus the imagined nature would not be established.
Therefore, these two natures are mutually dependent and lack priority or posteriority, because they arise from one another.

Since the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent, the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*) does not exist; as both are simultaneously absent, this is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).

Second, regarding cause and effect, one distinguishes that there is no priority or posteriority between them: if the cause were fixedly prior, it would not constitute a cause unless it itself had a cause.
If causes existed spontaneously without causal conditions, then causes would be infinite.
If the effect were definitively prior, then in the absence of a cause, it could not become an effect.
If an effect existed spontaneously without causes and conditions, the effects would be infinite.

Therefore, cause and effect have no fixed status; they are related to one another in a continuous succession. Relative to what precedes, it is the effect; relative to what follows, it is the cause. Thus, birth and death have no beginning.

In this way, the essence of cause and effect is precisely the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*). Since the imagined is non-existent and the dependent does not exist, this is suchness (*tathatā*).
Third, regarding the distinction of birth and cessation as having no priority or posteriority: if birth were prior and cessation posterior, there would be two faults:
first, that one would already undergo birth even before aging and death have occurred; second, that one would attain that subsequent birth even before relinquishing this present birth.
If that were so, there would be two further faults:
first, arising would be useless; since it has already arisen, what need is there for it to arise again?
This is because its retribution has not yet been relinquished.
Second, if birth were endless—where having been born, one is born again and again in succession—how could it ever come to an end?
If that were so, there would be two further fallacies:
first, if there were only birth and no cessation, it would follow that it is eternal; second, if there were multiple births, it would follow that there are multiple sentient beings.
If that were so, there would be no sense of cause and effect arising from one another; furthermore, if things were constantly arising, there would be no nirvana.
If cessation occurred first and arising followed later, then since arising had not yet occurred, what would there be for cessation to cease?
Furthermore, it would follow that one must first attain nirvāṇa and subsequently undergo birth and death, because cessation would exist prior [to arising].
This would mean that one who has already attained liberation would again fall back into bondage.
Therefore, arising and cessation have no sequence of before and after; nor are they separate from the imagined (parikalpita) and the dependent (paratantra). Hence, it is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
Regarding the two aspects of *tathatā* (suchness): this refers to the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and of phenomena.
There are three reasons why these two aspects of emptiness are called *tathatā*:
first, they are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
"Proliferation" (*prapañca*) refers to the adherence to the identity or difference of the ultimate and the conventional, and so forth.
The four types of denial are collectively termed proliferation.

If one were to hold that the ultimate and the conventional are definitively identical, then there would be no need for the cultivation of the path, as all would be liberated simultaneously; since everyone would perceive the ultimate, all would be noble ones (*ārya*).
Furthermore, if the ultimate and the conventional were definitively one, then the ultimate could not eliminate the conventional meaning.

Since it could not eliminate the conventional, the delusions of the conventional would not be removed, and there would be no possibility of liberation; there would be only ordinary beings and no noble ones.

If one holds that the ultimate is definitively different from the conventional, then by relying on the conventional one cannot penetrate the ultimate; the ultimate would thus be inaccessible because there would be no means for such access.
Therefore, the two kinds of emptiness are free from this conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and are thus called *tathatā* (suchness).
Second is the realm of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
This wisdom is free from inversion; since there is no conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) capable of serving as its object, that which this wisdom realizes is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
Third is true reality (*tathatā*).
If one contravenes this nature, one undergoes birth and death; if one accords with this nature, one attains nirvana.
This nature is the true nature of all phenomena; therefore, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Therefore, these two are called the suchness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatathatā*).
It is not that characteristics are empty of expression; rather, it is by means of the emptiness of characteristics that they constitute characteristics.
Regarding the suchness of the three consciousnesses (*vijñanatathatā*), it means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are merely consciousness alone.
This consciousness possesses two meanings, and for this reason it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*):
first, it encompasses non-perversion; second, it is without change.

Regarding the encompassing of non-perversion: it means that all phenomena, such as the twelve bases (*āyatana*), are nothing but consciousness alone, because apart from the deluded consciousness there are no other separate phenomena.
All dharmas are subsumed within consciousness; this principle is definitive, and thus it is called "unerring subsumption. Because it is unerring, it is suchness (*tathatā*).
However, this unerring suchness is not yet the suchness of signlessness (*animitta-tathatā*).

"Non-alteration" clarifies that this deluded consciousness is manifested as the discriminating and the dependent consciousnesses that resemble external objects. Because the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is eternally non-existent, the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*) also does not exist. That these two are non-existent is precisely the *amala-vijñāna* (immaculate consciousness); because only this consciousness alone is without alteration, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*).
Previously, when "suchness" (tathatā) was mentioned, it merely eliminated the twelve bases (āyatana).
According to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), all dharmas are analyzed as being solely the twelve bases, which they hold to be non-perverted.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna doctrine, all bases are refuted as being entirely non-existent, for they are produced solely by the deluded consciousness.
The twelve bases (*āyatana*) constitute inversion; only the single disordered consciousness (*vikṣipta-vijñāna*) is not inverted, and is therefore called *tathatā* (suchness).

Although the substance of this consciousness still undergoes transformation, one next employs the *parikalpita* (imagined) and *paratantra* (dependent) [natures] to eliminate this disordered consciousness. Only the *amala-vijñāna* (immaculate consciousness) is non-inverted and non-transforming; it is true *tathatā*.

In the preceding discussion on the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra*, one should likewise employ this teaching of consciousness: first, the single deluded consciousness (*bhrānti-vijñāna*) is used to dispel external objects; next, the *amala-vijñāna* (immaculate consciousness) is used to dispel the deluded consciousness; thus, ultimately, there is only the single pure consciousness.
The fourth reliance, suchness, refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
There are three aspects of the truth of suffering:
first, the category of suffering; second, the truth of suffering; and third, the noble truth of suffering (*ārya-duḥkha-satya*).
Regarding the category of suffering (*duḥkhagati*): it refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). Based on these five, one is designated as a "sentient being.
Since there is nothing that serves as the basis for suffering apart from these five, they are called the category of suffering.

Regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): it refers to non-perversion; it clarifies that this category of suffering is definitively contrary to the intent of the Noble Ones (*ārya*). Because this meaning is real, it is called the Truth of Suffering.
The Sage, relying upon this, resolutely gives rise to renunciation and does not produce defiled attachment.
As for the Noble Truth of Suffering, it refers to the single flavor of suffering.

One clarifies that this Truth of Suffering is empty because it lacks intrinsic nature; being empty, it is signless; being signless, it is wishless, such that there is not a single dharma to be wished for or sought after.

This is explained according to their common characteristics: the essence of the three liberations is in fact one; since all phenomena do not transcend this, they are called "of one flavor" (*ekarasa*), which is the correct meaning of "saintly" (*ārya*).
This single flavor is non-erroneous and unchanging; therefore, it is called the Noble Truth (*āryasatya*).
The first category of suffering is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*);

the subsequent truth of suffering is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), for being non-erroneous constitutes the establishment of the ultimate truth. The final one is the truth of the ultimate meaning (*paramārthasatya*), which, being non-erroneous and without variation, is the non-conceptualized truth (*avyavasthāpanasatya*).
The same applies to the three truths that follow.
Regarding the suchness of the fivefold wrong practice, this refers to the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Following the pattern of suffering, there are likewise three aspects:

First is the category of accumulation (*samudaya-varga*), which refers to the six types of craving that arise based on the six sense objects; these are capable of causing the continuity of birth and death, such that one does not transcend this category.
Second is the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*), which refers to knowing [this] without inversion.
These six types of craving certainly cause the continuity of existence; being true and non-erroneous, they are called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Regarding the third Noble Truth of Origination: its single flavor is not different from the preceding Four Truths, for it shares with them the single flavor of the three doors of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*).
The sixth, the suchness of purity, refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
It also has three aspects:
first, the category of cessation (*nirodha-jāti*), which refers to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; that is, the complete extinction and non-arising of the two delusions of views and thought.
The second, the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), refers to non-perversion.
That this category of cessation is definitively quiescent is its meaning as a "truth.
The third, the noble truth of cessation (*ārya-nirodha-satya*), refers to the single flavor of cessation, which is not different from the former.
The seventh, the suchness of right practice, refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
It also has three aspects:
first, the category of the path, which refers to the eightfold noble path as its constituent categories.
Regarding the second, the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), it refers to being non-erroneous.
These eight [factors] are definitively able to lead to deliverance from the origin of suffering; this is the meaning of "truth" (*satya*).
Regarding the third, the Noble Truth of the Path, it means that the path has a single flavor and is not different from what preceded it.
Furthermore, that which relies upon suchness is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
The Truth of Suffering refers to the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because they are impermanent (*anitya*).
Impermanence has three meanings:
First, there is non-existence and impermanence: this refers to the fact that the nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is eternally non-existent;
this non-existence is the meaning of impermanence. That this non-existence truly exists is called suchness (*tathatā*).

If one considers that which was previously non-existent and subsequently non-existent to be impermanence, this is merely conventional truth; it is called "suchness" (tathatā) in the sense of being non-perverted, but it is not true suchness.
Second is the impermanence of arising and ceasing, which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as suffering.

This dependent nature is neither truly existent nor truly non-existent: it is not truly existent because it differs from the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and it is not truly non-existent because it differs from the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Because it is not substantially existent, it is cessation; because it is not substantially non-existent, it is arising.
Such arising and cessation constitute the meaning of impermanence, yet this arising is not real arising and this cessation is not real cessation—this is the suchness of suchness.
Third is impermanence characterized by both detachment and non-detachment, which refers to the true nature of suffering (*duḥkha-tattva*).

This nature is not free from defilement prior to the Path, but is free from defilement subsequent to the Path; it is called "impermanent" because its status is not fixed across these stages, yet it is named "Suchness" (*tathatā*) because its essence does not undergo change.
Furthermore, the suchness of wrong practice refers to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The Truth of Origination consists of two types: the true origination and the semblance origination.
True origination refers to the fact that the various afflictions (*kleśa*) cause the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to continue in existence.
"Resembling accumulation" refers to various karmas that can bring about the distinctions among the various paths.
There are three kinds of accumulation:

first, accumulated through perfuming (*vāsanā*), which refers to the delusions of the nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) that are able to perfume and give rise to accumulation.
Why is this? Because the afflictions categorized as conceptualization (*vikalpa*) act as the cause for the accumulation [of suffering].
Second, there is the origination of accumulation, which refers to both afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma (*karman*).
Why is this? Because it arises through formation.
The commentary states:

This origination of arising is precisely the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); the essence of the dependent nature consists of afflictions and karma, through which this nature can give rise to the future self-substance of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Furthermore, as for the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), that which is produced is itself self-produced; because it produces others, it is called "arising" (*samudaya*).
The Treatise says:
"The inseparable triad of arising refers to the arising of *tathatā* (suchness)."
This essence of suchness (tathatā), when not yet free from obscurations, is called "accumulation" (saṃcaya). Why is this?
Because this suchness is the nature of that which accumulates and is that which is obscured by accumulation; therefore, it is called the "suchness of accumulation."
These three are precisely the three natures of non-substantiality; therefore, they are called suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, pure suchness refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
It also possesses three meanings:
First, the non-arising and non-ceasing of essential nature (*svabhāva*): this means that the delusions of the conceptualizing class (*vikalpa-varga*) have no essential nature from the beginning;

therefore, they are called "ceasing. Second, the non-arising and non-ceasing of the grasper: this means that the delusions of the class of distracted consciousness (*bhrānti-vijñāna*) arise only through causes and conditions and have no origination from the beginning; therefore, they are called "ceasing."
The two types of extinction of the three impurities refer to primordial purity (*prakṛti-vyavadāna*) and stainless purity (*vaimalya-vyavadāna*).
Primordial purity is explained in terms of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), while stainless purity is explained in terms of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Why is this? Because this nature possesses a substantial essence, it is capable of being defiled; yet, because impurities are removed by the Path, it attains purity.
Original purity refers to the state prior to and during the Path, while stainless purity refers to the state subsequent to the Path.

These two purities are also called the two kinds of nirvāṇa. The former is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); it is inherently present by its own nature and is not obtained through wisdom.
The latter is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); it is obtained through the cultivation of the path.

In view of what precedes, it is called "primordially existent" (*pūrvam-bhava*); in view of what follows, it is called "initially existent. Because its initial manifestation is termed "initial existence," it is called the "pure suchness" (*viśuddha-tathatā*).
Furthermore, the suchness of correct practice refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
There are also three meanings:

first, "knowing the path," which refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Since this nature has no substantial essence, one must simply know that there is nothing to be extinguished; therefore, it is called "knowing the path."

Second is the path of elimination (*prahāṇa-mārga*). With respect to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), this nature possesses substantial reality; therefore, one should know that it belongs to the category of afflictions and must be extinguished. For this reason, it is called the path of elimination.

Third is the realization of the path. With respect to the nature of reality (*tathatā*), since this nature consists of the two kinds of emptiness, one should know that it is to be attained through the elimination [of afflictions and obstacles].
Therefore, it is called the "suchness of correct practice."
The essence of these seven kinds of true reality consists of the three non-natures; therefore, they are collectively termed *tathatā* (suchness).
Among these seven, the first three are non-positively established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
Why is this? Because these three possess only distinct names but no distinct substantial entities.
The reason that suchness-as-arising (*tathatā-utpāda*) is placed first is because it is that which can be eliminated.
The reason the *tathatā* of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-tathatā*) occupies the second position is that it is the same as the arising family in its cessation.
The reason the *tathatā* of consciousness (*vijñāna-tathatā*) is placed last is that it is the skillful means for the cessation of that [arising family].
The latter four are established as such according to the truths of formal establishment (*vyavasthāna-satya*). Why is this?
These four are designated by name according to their function (*kāritra*), for there are four functions.
The name is not established based on its essence, because the essence is of a single flavor.
One should know that the reason "reliance" (*āśraya*) is mentioned first is for the sake of seeing.
There are two meanings to be understood:
First, the objects of knowledge are manifold; second, one need only know these and there is no further meaning beyond them.

Regarding the manifoldness of the objects of knowledge: within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), there are four types of meanings—impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*).
Regarding the remaining three truths—origination and so forth—they possess only four names but no difference in their four meanings.

Why is this? Because the truth of origination is real only in the sense of being a cause; the truth of cessation is real only in the sense of tranquility; and the truth of the path is real only in the sense of renunciation.
The remaining nine meanings, such as "having an object" (*sālambana*), are all merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

Regarding the point that one need only know these two and that there are no further meanings: suffering is the fruit of karma; since it is a retribution (*vipāka*) and not an affliction (*kleśa*), it cannot be eliminated.
Since it is not a supreme excellence (*guṇa*), it does not need to be realized.
Since it is not correct practice, there is no need to cultivate it;
however, it must be understood for the sake of wearying detachment (nirveda), and therefore there is no further sense of abandonment, realization, or cultivation.
If one knows this, one is able to eliminate all afflictions; therefore, wrong conduct is placed second.
Because afflictions are eliminated, one realizes purity; therefore, purity is placed third.
Because one has realized the perfection of purity, right practice is fulfilled.
Why is this? For the Path has three functions:
First, one perceives the true meaning; second, one eliminates unwholesome phenomena; third, one is able to reach tranquility.
When these three are fully possessed, the function of the path is perfected; therefore, it is said that right practice occurs in the fourth [stage].
These seven suchnesses are precisely the nature of reality (*tathatā*).
(From the *Treatise on the Three Non-natures*, Vol. Upper and Vol. Lower, excerpted from the *Treatise on the Signless*).
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, while translating at Zhizhi Temple in Guangzhou, was asked:
"How are these seven included within the nature of reality (*tathatā*)? He replied:
These seven are thus praiseworthy because they are the sphere of the two supreme types of knowledge (*jñāna*).
These two types of knowledge are the knowledge of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā-jñāna*) and the knowledge of things in their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā-jñāna*).
This knowledge is praiseworthy because it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and transcends that of ordinary persons; it is supreme because it surpasses that of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
Furthermore, it is praiseworthy because it is the wisdom of a bodhisattva, and it is supreme because it is the wisdom of a Buddha.
This reveals the meaning of non-erroneousness, for it is the objective domain of non-erroneous wisdom.
Furthermore, because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), it is called "reality" (*tattva*).
To be free from conceptual proliferation means to be free from the false notions of identity and difference regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
"Characteristics and so forth" refers to the four categories—characteristics, names, discrimination, and correct knowledge—which constitute four of the five dharma-treasuries.
Why is it that they cannot be said to be either identical or different?
Because both positions entail faults.
If True Suchness were different from the characteristics and so forth, there would be three faults:
First, this suchness is not a substantial entity characterized by marks;
second, the practitioner cultivating contemplation does not rely on marks as a means to attain penetration into suchness;
third, once suchness has been realized, one should not have attained [the realization of] phenomena characterized by marks, because they are mutually unrelated.
If true suchness (*tathatā*) and the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) were one and the same, there would likewise be three faults:
first, since true suchness is without differentiation, the marks should also be without differentiation;
second, if one sees the marks, one would immediately see true suchness.

Third, if one perceives True Suchness (tathatā) as being unable to purify itself—just as one perceives the marks of phenomena (nimitta)—then there would be no noble ones (ārya), no attainment of liberation, no nirvāṇa, and no distinction between the mundane and the supramundane.
